parts: THE COAT
This breed does not need elaborate styling. The key to grooming is maintaining the coat's length, with particular attention to its fullness and volume.

By parting the coat in lines, you can see the "undercoat" or "wool" beneath, which protects the dog's skin. The Bobtail's long, thick coat is a natural adaptation that insulates the dog against cold and rain in winter and protects against the sun's rays in summer.

The Bobtail has a long, harsh coat with a strong texture. It should be abundant, but not so full that the dog appears overweight. It is neither straight nor curly, but slightly wavy, and should be free of tangles and mats. Coat quality and texture are more important than thickness. A soft or sleek coat is considered a fault. The undercoat should be waterproof unless it has been removed through combing or natural shedding.
Bobtail puppies have soft, short coats that are easy to brush. As they grow, however, their dense adult coats develop and things change. Without regular grooming (twice a week), tangles can form.
BRUSHING

Help your puppy get used to grooming from a very young age. When the coat starts to change, at around seven months of age, use the comb more often to remove dead hair. Do not rush or brush forcefully. Work slowly and gently to avoid breaking the ends.

Once the coat has changed completely, use a new brush regularly rather than a comb, reserving the comb for the area above the muzzle and the lower legs. Choose a good brush with iron pins or metal pins set in a rubber cushion (without balls on the tips), or a natural-bristle brush. Never use a slicker brush: it pulls out too much hair and, although the finish may look perfect, it can damage the undercoat.
For grooming the moustache, beard and hair beneath the ears, use a metal comb with thick, widely spaced teeth and rounded tips.

Brushing too often can damage the undercoat, while leaving too long between sessions can cause matting. An adult Bobtail should be brushed once a week and checked daily. Gently separate any tangles with your fingers, never with a comb; use the comb only after the tangle has been removed, to clear away broken hairs. For stubborn tangles that cannot be worked out by hand, use only the first tooth of the comb. Hold the hair at its base with your left hand and gently tease out the tangle so that you do not pull on the dog's skin.

Grooming is quicker for dogs that are not shown, as the undercoat can be combed out. In show dogs, however, the undercoat must be kept in the best possible condition, and any tangles should be removed carefully to avoid damaging it.
Hair that falls heavily over the eyes and blocks vision can be gathered into a ponytail using a suitable hair band.
If your Bobtail's coat gets muddy, wait until it is completely dry. The dirt will then be easier to brush out.
A chamois cloth can be used to dry a wet coat.

The hair around the anal area, which often becomes soiled when the dog passes stools, needs checking almost daily. Remove any stuck-on faeces with an iron comb with long, narrow teeth reserved specifically for this purpose.
Some breeders and groomers use talcum powder to clean the coat. This practice is strongly discouraged, as the powder can irritate the skin, clog pores and hinder normal skin function.

To make brushing easier, get your Bobtail used to staying still on a grooming table. With the dog lying first on one side and then the other, groom the legs and sides of the body. Then, with the dog standing, finish the head and back.
First brush the coat in one direction. Then, to position it correctly, back-brush the areas that need lift. Brush in the following directions:
Head: from back to front.
Ears: from the base to the tip.
Neck and chest: from top to bottom.
Sides of the neck and front sections of the sides: from top to bottom.
Back of the neck and front of the back: towards the tail.
Belly: downwards.
Rear of the back and rear sections of the sides: towards the head.
Legs: from bottom to top.
Hindquarters: upwards.

As mentioned earlier, an excessively full coat distorts the dog's outline. Adding shapeless bulk only detracts from the dog's appearance when judged. This fault can be partly corrected by skilfully shaping the coat, a delicate task requiring experience and careful attention to preserving the features specified in the breed standard. Scissors or similar tools should never be used for this grooming.
BATHING
As a general rule, dogs can be bathed every two months in lukewarm water, using a suitable shampoo that will not harm their skin.
For a show Bobtail, or to keep the coat in the best possible condition, occasional bathing only when needed is recommended. Thorough brushing once a week will keep the coat clean.

Bear in mind that bathing alters this breed's coat, making it too soft and reducing the undercoat's waterproofing. Washing encourages growth but worsens texture, so bathe only when strictly necessary. When you do, thoroughly detangle the coat beforehand and dry it completely afterwards. Brush as you dry, smoothing the hair on the neck while drying the head and legs against the direction of growth. Brush thoroughly again after 24 hours; otherwise, tangles can form that are almost impossible to remove.

Do not bathe dogs that are unwell, pregnant females or puppies undergoing their vaccination course. Avoid bathing if you cannot be sure of keeping the dog from becoming chilled, as this can happen easily.

The Bobtail is a British breed, and in Britain it is shown with a more natural appearance, achieving the required shape through brushing alone. The head and rump are backcombed, and the coat is often presented with a centre parting.
I believe these traditional methods, so true to the breed, should be respected, as they help us preserve the authentic Bobtail.
EARS, TEETH AND NAILS
The ears should be free of hair to help prevent infections and hearing loss. Do not trim the hair yourself unless you know how to do so properly. Ask your breeder or vet for guidance.

Brushing your dog's teeth is beneficial. There are several ways to do it, and the best approach depends on what works for you and your dog. Some dogs dislike having something put in their mouths, but brushing is still important. Be gentle and speak reassuringly. Ask your vet how to proceed safely to avoid being bitten. Do not feed your dog human food; dog food is made for dogs and helps clean their teeth.

Your dog's nails should be trimmed monthly. If allowed to grow too long, they can cause the toes to splay and affect posture. Trim carefully to avoid the "quick", the pink, living part of the nail. If accidentally cut, it will bleed, much as your cuticle would if trimmed too closely. The quick is visible as a pink area in white nails, but with dark nails you must trim only a very small amount at a time.
